name: ensemble-and-multirate
title: Ensemble throughput and multi-rate scheduling
question: When many instances of the monolithic model are run together, (a) as a same-rate parameter ensemble does vivarium orchestration on a real parallel backend (Ray) deliver a genuine throughput speedup, and (b) as a genuinely multi-rate ensemble (each instance on a different interval) does process-bigraph #270's event-heap scheduler beat the stock scan loop as the process count grows, while staying bit-identical?
hypothesis: A Ray-backed same-rate ensemble of monoliths delivers a real wall-clock speedup (libroadrunner does not release the GIL, so only OS-process parallelism helps); and the #270 heap scheduler runs the SAME math as the scan loop (bit-identical) with a wall-clock advantage that grows with the instance count P on a multi-rate ensemble.
objective: Fan the monolith out into same-rate and multi-rate ensembles and measure the real Ray speedup and the heap-vs-scan scheduler advantage.
description: Methods study of the SBML-decomposition investigation on Teusink glycolysis (BIOMD0000000064, 17 floating species), merging two ensemble questions on the generic ensemble composite. SAME-RATE (intervals unset): N monolithic Tellurium instances run concurrently via Ray OS processes with parameter draws. MULTI-RATE (intervals=geometric): N independent monolithic instances, each advanced on a different geometrically-spaced interval, run under scheduler=scan (stock O(P^2) tick loop) and scheduler=heap (#270 event-heap, O(P log P)); the instances share no store and are uncoupled, so there is no splitting error and only the scheduler changes.
claim: A Ray ensemble of monoliths gives a real 7.5x wall-clock speedup on 16 cores — the one study where vivarium wins on speed; libroadrunner does NOT release the GIL, so in-process threads cannot (they backfire). Separately, process-bigraph #270's event-heap scheduler is bit-identical to the stock scan loop (same math, different tick order) and its wall-clock advantage grows monotonically with P on a genuinely multi-rate composite — measured 0.98x at P=4 (heap bookkeeping with nothing to gain), crossing over near P~50-64, to 1.64x at P=256 on real libroadrunner/CVODE instances. The per-process CVODE integration dominates the per-tick scan until P reaches the low hundreds, so the multiplier is modest at the P a unit test can afford; it is reported as measured, and the regime where it grows large (hundreds-to-thousands of cheap processes) is #270's own 4.8x@P=100 -> 46x@P=1000 micro-benchmark, cited not reproduced.

expected_behavior.name: ray-ensemble-real-parallel-speedup
expected_behavior.condition: speedup > 1 on a multi-core host via Ray OS processes, or an explicit serial-fallback declaring no speedup
expected_behavior.rationale: the ensemble study must show a genuine parallel win, not a mislabeled serial loop.

expected_behavior.name: heap-beats-scan-at-scale
expected_behavior.observable: scan (stock O(P^2)) vs heap (#270 O(P log P)) run wall-clock, and their speedup, vs the instance count P
expected_behavior.condition: scan and heap produce bit-identical final state at every P (same math, different scheduler); the heap/scan speedup rises monotonically with P and exceeds 1 at the largest measured P (heap faster)
expected_behavior.rationale: a many-rate composite is exactly the O(P^2) case the event-heap scheduler was built to fix; because only the tick ordering changes, correctness must be identical and only wall-clock may differ.

findings.summary: [same-rate/Ray] n_instances=8, 16 CPUs: serial 1.189s → Ray 0.158s = 7.52x real speedup (backend=ray, speedup_claimed=true).

[same-rate/Ray] libroadrunner does NOT release the GIL during .simulate() (8-instance ThreadPool = 0.99x), so Ray's separate OS processes are the only path; in-process parallel_processes backfires for this CVODE-wrapping work.

[multi-rate/heap] Scan and heap are bit-identical at every measured P — multirate_scaling records a per-N bit_identical flag (np.array_equal of the two schedulers' final state across every instance store), True at each of P=4..256, and a dedicated test asserts it across the measured Ns (not just the small-N case). #270 changes only the order in which due processes are popped, never the math. The multi-rate composite is uncoupled (independent monoliths, empty inputs), so there is no split-coupling divergence to confound the timing.

[multi-rate/heap] Measured scan vs heap run() wall-clock (median of 3, construction excluded), geometric intervals i_fast=H/(3P)..i_slow=3H, H=20: P=4 scan=0.0082s heap=0.0083s (0.98x); P=16 0.0468s / 0.0492s (0.95x); P=64 0.419s / 0.371s (1.13x); P=128 1.555s / 1.280s (1.22x); P=256 6.598s / 4.019s (1.64x). The heap/scan speedup rises monotonically with P and crosses over near P~50-64.

[multi-rate/heap] Honesty: heap is ~5% SLOWER at tiny P (P=4,16) — the event-heap bookkeeping has nothing to gain when the per-tick scan is trivially short — exactly #270's documented single-rate penalty. The win is modest (<=1.64x) at the P a test can afford because the real libroadrunner/CVODE update per due process dominates the per-tick Python scan at small P (measured crossover ~P=50-64). #270's cheap-process micro-benchmark (where the scheduler is the whole cost) is 4.8x@P=100 rising to 46x@P=1000; ensemble-and-multirate reproduces the TREND with real integrator instances, not those multipliers.

[multi-rate/heap] Scheduler API used (#270): the strategy is the "scheduler" CONFIG FIELD on the Composite (Composite({"state": doc, "scheduler": "heap"|"scan"|"auto"}, core=core)); "auto" (the default) picks heap only when more than one distinct process interval is present. ensemble-and-multirate selects "scan" vs "heap" explicitly to measure both.
